what_it_does: Today's internet security relies on math problems — like factoring huge numbers — that classical computers cannot solve in any reasonable time. A powerful enough quantum computer could break those problems in hours, rendering today's encrypted communications vulnerable. Governments and standards bodies have already published replacements (called post-quantum cryptography, or PQC), but the challenge is knowing where the old, fragile algorithms are hiding in complex software stacks, supply chains, and internet protocols. This invited paper introduces Quartz, a tool that maps out where quantum-unsafe cryptography is used by building a dependency graph — think of it as a wiring diagram — showing which components rely on which encryption methods and how risk propagates. It can also automatically produce a "Cryptography Bill of Materials" (CBOM), similar to a software bill of materials, listing all cryptographic ingredients in a system so organizations can prioritize what to replace. The paper appears to be a position and tool-description piece rather than a benchmarked system; concrete performance claims would need the full paper.
